summary: Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, presents on why vertical AI agents need more than chat interfaces. He opens with a relatable failure mode: a long-running agent that researches, drafts, compacts context, forgets everything, and produces a flawed contract — then repeats poorly after feedback. Legora is a collaborative AI workspace for law firms with 1,000+ customers across 50+ markets, growing extremely fast. The core thesis is that economics of production have shifted: doing work is now cheap, but planning and reviewing work are the new bottlenecks. Lauritzen references the verifier's rule (coined by Jason): if a task is solvable and easy to verify, AI will eventually solve it. Different verticals and tasks fall at different points on the verifiability spectrum — checking contract definitions is easy to verify; writing a contract is easy to solve but hard to verify; litigation strategy is nearly impossible to verify. He identifies two dimensions of agent-human collaboration: trust (how much review is needed) and control (how effectively a human can steer the agent). To increase trust, he suggests bringing tasks down the verifiability spectrum, using proxy verification (golden contracts), decomposing tasks so humans handle judgment-heavy parts, and adding guardrails. To increase control, he evaluates planning (inefficient, blind to contingencies), skills (encoding human judgment at work nodes with contingency handling), and elicitation (asking the human when unsure, with self-unblocking and a decision log). He argues chat is one-dimensional, low-bandwidth, and unsuitable for large work trees. In the final section, he offers concrete alternatives: persistent artifacts that vary by vertical. A document is a durable interface where users highlight specific clauses, add comments, tag agents and collaborators, and hand off parts to specialized agents. Legora's tabular review is a known primitive where the agent reviews contracts, flags items needing human judgment, enables quick review, and then proceeds. He notes chat as input is great (flexible, voice-enabled) but should not be the main collaboration mode. He closes with the insight that language is the universal interface for humans, but agents aren't humans and should not be constrained to human language.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The economics of production have shifted: doing work is now cheap, but planning and reviewing work are the new bottlenecks for complex agents.
The verifier's rule states that if a task is solvable and easy to verify, AI will solve it; verifiability varies across tasks and industries.
Trust (how much review is needed) and control (how effectively a human can steer the agent) are the two key dimensions of agent-human collaboration.
Trust can be increased through proxy verification, task decomposition, and guardrails; control through planning, skills, and elicitation with decision logs.
Chat is one-dimensional and low-bandwidth, collapsing complex work trees into linear sequences — it should not be the main collaboration mode for complex agents.
Persistent, high-bandwidth artifacts like documents and tabular reviews enable targeted collaboration: highlighting clauses, tagging agents, flagging items for human judgment.
Chat as input is valuable (flexible, voice-enabled) but agents aren't humans and should not be constrained to human language interfaces.
High-bandwidth artifacts should be persistent and will look different industry to industry depending on the task being solved.
Understand the shifted economics of production where planning and reviewing, not doing, are the new bottlenecks.

sections.title: Introduction and the long-running agent problem
sections.summary: Jacob introduces himself and Legora, then illustrates the painful experience of a long-running complex agent that drafts a contract over 30 minutes, compacts its context, forgets everything, and fails to make targeted fixes on retry.

sections.title: Legora background and the goal of vertical AI
sections.summary: Legora is a collaborative AI workspace for law firms with 1,000+ customers across 50+ markets, growing extremely fast. The goal of most vertical AI companies is to make agents complete more complex work end-to-end.

sections.title: New economics of production and the verifier's rule
sections.summary: The bottleneck has shifted from doing work (now cheap) to planning and reviewing work. The verifier's rule (coined by Jason) states that if a task is solvable and easy to verify, AI will solve it. Different industries and tasks fall at different points on the verifiability spectrum — legal definition checking is easy, contract writing is hard to verify, litigation strategy is nearly impossible.

sections.title: Trust and how to increase it
sections.summary: Trust determines how much review is needed. Methods to increase trust include bringing tasks down the verifiability spectrum (TDD, browser access), using proxy verification (golden contracts), decomposing tasks to separate judgment-heavy parts from verifiable parts, and adding guardrails to limit agent scope.

sections.title: Control and how to increase it: planning, skills, elicitation
sections.summary: Control is how effectively a human can steer the agent. Planning aligns on approach upfront but is inefficient and blind to contingencies. Skills encode human judgment at work nodes and handle contingencies but don't cover everything. Elicitation asks the human when unsure, ideally with self-unblocking and a decision log for later review.

sections.title: Chat is inadequate — high-bandwidth artifacts needed
sections.summary: Chat is one-dimensional and low-bandwidth, collapsing complex work trees into linear sequences. For large work trees with many questions, chat becomes unmanageable. Lauritzen proposes that humans and agents should collaborate in high-bandwidth artifacts instead.

sections.title: Concrete artifacts: documents, tabular review, and agents beyond human language
sections.summary: Lauritzen gives concrete examples of high-bandwidth artifacts. A document is a persistent, durable interface where users highlight specific clauses to change only them, add comments, tag agents and collaborators, and hand off parts to specialized agents. Legora's tabular review is a known primitive where the agent reviews contracts, flags items for human judgment, enables quick high-control review, then proceeds. He notes chat as input is great (flexible, voice-enabled) but should not be the main collaboration mode. He closes with the insight that language is the universal interface for humans — he recounts wishing he could draw an org chart for a candidate instead of describing it verbally — but agents aren't humans and should not be constrained to human language.

demonstrations: Opening anecdote: long-running agent drafts a contract, compacts context, forgets everything, and fails to fix only the requested clause on retry.
Coding example: giving an agent browser access and using test-driven development makes feature implementation verifiable.
Legal example: comparing a new contract to golden contracts (known-good precedents) as a proxy for verification.
Contract task decomposition: leaving risk profile, precedent selection, and negotiation stance to humans while agents handle formatting and definition linting.
Claude Code guardrail spectrum: low-trust mode asks permission for everything; high-trust YOLO mode lets it run freely.
Document as durable interface: highlight clause three to change only clause three, add comments, tag agents and collaborators, hand off parts to special agents.
Tabular review: agent spins up a known primitive, reviews all contracts, flags items for human judgment, enables quick review, then kicks off the rest of the agent.
Org chart anecdote: Jacob wished he could draw an org chart for a candidate instead of describing it in language — illustrating human limitations that agents need not share.
limitations: Chat is one-dimensional and low-bandwidth, unsuitable for complex multi-step agent work trees.
Planning requires doing the work upfront to know what to plan and cannot handle contingencies discovered during execution.
You don't have skills for everything, so skills alone cannot fully solve the control problem.
Some tasks like litigation strategy are nearly impossible to verify because there is no objective truth.
Contract verification is only truly possible when a judge rules in court, making it impractical for iterative agent loops.
Humans are limited by language as a communication interface, but agents are not humans and should not be constrained to the same limitation.
